title: Browser trust boundaries across DOM sinks, origins, and framing

threat_model.actor: Anyone who can place content the page later renders, host a document that frames or messages the application, or induce a user to visit a page they control
threat_model.asset: The application's origin: its DOM, its cookies and storage, and any action the user's session can perform from it
threat_model.trust_boundary: The origin that authored a script or a message and the origin whose authority it ends up executing with
threat_model.failure_mode: Content reaches a sink that parses it as markup or script, or a cross-document channel accepts a peer it never actually identified, or an isolation attribute is granted away
threat_model.impact: Script runs in the application's origin, or a foreign document drives privileged behaviour, reads state, or captures user intent

required_evidence: The application renders content in a browser and at least some of that content originates outside the codebase
A client-side trust decision exists: a rendering sink, a cross-document channel, a framing policy, or a storage read

signals: Markup is assembled as a string and assigned to a parsing sink rather than built as nodes
An escaping helper handles element text but the value is interpolated into an attribute or a URL position
A URL is written to href, src, or an action attribute without a scheme allowlist
A framework escape hatch for raw HTML is used for content the server did not author
A dynamic component, tag, or property name is chosen from data rather than from a fixed map
Server-rendered state is embedded in the page as script rather than as inert data
The message origin is compared with a prefix, a substring, or a regular expression instead of an exact match
The sending window is never compared with the frame the application created
A reply is posted with a wildcard target origin, or carries state the peer should not receive
A sandbox attribute grants allow-scripts together with allow-same-origin
An isolation attribute is applied after the content is assigned or after the element joins the document
A content security policy allows unsafe-inline, or is delivered only on some responses
A message handler admits an origin by prefix and dispatches to a privileged command table
A preview renders unsanitised markup into a frame whose sandbox is granted away

boundary.subject: the origin that authored the content or the message
boundary.object: the DOM, storage, and session authority of the application's origin
boundary.invariant: Content that the application did not author never becomes script or markup in the application's origin, and every cross-document peer is identified exactly before it is trusted

examples: Function constructor or timer string argument
State restored from storage and rendered

signals: Enumerate every parsing and URL sink and trace each argument back to whoever authored it
Check the escaping context at each interpolation: element text, attribute value, URL, and script positions are different problems
Read every isolation attribute together with where and when it is applied relative to content assignment and insertion
State which origins may message the application and compare that with the comparison the handler performs
Decide what a message peer is permitted to do and compare it with the command table it can reach
Establish whether the policy header, sandbox attribute, or framing rule is delivered on every response that matters
Identify stored fields rendered into markup or URL positions later, especially profile and comment content
Determine what the page keeps in client storage and whether it is rendered back without treatment
Load the page locally, send messages from a controlled document, and record which origins and command names are accepted
Render a benign marker payload through the suspected sink and observe whether it is parsed or shown as text

steps: Confirm explicit authorization and run against a local build with synthetic content only
Render a benign marker through the ordinary feature first, so a later difference is attributable to the payload
Use an inert marker that proves parsing without exfiltration, and never target a live user or a third-party site
Send messages from a locally controlled document with related and unrelated origins, and record which are accepted
Record the sink, the escaping context, the delivered policy headers, and the isolation attributes actually present at load time

false_positive_filters: The value is inserted as a text node or through a framework binding that escapes for the context it lands in
The markup is produced by a sanitizer whose configuration and output context have been read, not assumed from its name
The framed content is isolated by a sandbox that grants neither scripts nor same-origin, applied before the content is assigned
A content security policy that actually blocks the sink is delivered on the response in question, evidenced by the header rather than a configuration file alone
The message handler compares the origin exactly and verifies the sending window, so a foreign document cannot be the peer
The sink is unreachable in the built bundle, or renders content the application itself authored

For a React 19 URL prop rendered by React itself, a local reproduction shows the javascript: value being replaced with React's inert blocked-URL error value before it reaches the document; this refutes script execution through that exact framework-rendered href/src sink only, not direct DOM setters, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, location/window navigation, another framework path, another scheme, or an open-redirect claim, and a scheme allowlist is still preferred hardening

The apparent URL source is an operator-controlled configuration boundary with no demonstrated attacker write path; until a user, tenant, external provider, or other untrusted actor can actually change that value, attacker control for the XSS claim is not established even if the value reaches a URL sink

required_evidence: The sink, the escaping context it lands in, and the author of the value that reaches it
A reachable path from a place an attacker can write to the render or the message handler
A local reproduction using an inert marker that shows the content being parsed rather than displayed
The defective invariant stated as an authorship or peer-identity failure, and what the executing content can reach
refutation_tests: Re-read the render for a text-node or framework-escaped path that the surrounding string building disguises
Check the delivered response headers for a policy that blocks the sink before asserting execution
Inspect the sandbox attribute value and the order of assignment before concluding framed content is contained
Send a message from an unrelated origin to confirm the handler's comparison really admits it

On an authorized local React 19 build, pass an inert javascript: marker through the exact React-rendered href/src prop, inspect the rendered attribute and execution result, and verify React neutralizes that sink; separately search for the same value reaching direct setAttribute/property assignment, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, location.assign, window.open, or another non-React path before refuting the candidate

Trace who can write the configuration value all the way to its source API/storage and attempt the lowest-privilege authorized write path; refute attacker control only when no untrusted identity or external provider can change it, and reopen the candidate if any alternate write path exists

root_causes: Markup is assembled as a string, so escaping must be correct for several contexts at once
An escaping helper written for element text is reused in attribute or URL positions
Origin checks use prefix or substring comparison, so a longer hostile hostname satisfies them
The sending window is never verified, so any document that can reach the page can be the peer
An isolation attribute grants scripts and same-origin together, or is applied after the content has been assigned
A privileged command table is reachable from a channel whose peer is a document rather than an authenticated caller

variant_strategy.result_contract: EXACT | VARIANT | REFUTED | BLOCKED; exact and variant matches remain hypotheses until verified

remediation.canonical_invariant: Build the DOM from nodes and validated URLs rather than from markup strings, and identify every cross-document peer exactly before granting it anything
patterns: Insert untrusted values as text nodes and set attributes through explicit APIs rather than through interpolation
Validate URL schemes against an allowlist before assigning any navigational attribute
Compare message origins with equality against a fixed list and verify the sending window, and reply to an exact origin
Keep cross-document channels limited to presentation commands, so a channel compromise cannot reach privileged operations
Render content that cannot be sanitized inside a frame whose sandbox grants neither scripts nor same-origin, set before the content is assigned
Deliver a content security policy without unsafe-inline as defence in depth, and verify it on the responses that carry the sink

assertions: The vulnerable bridge admits an origin that merely begins with the trusted origin and reaches a privileged command table
The vulnerable bridge replies with a wildcard target origin carrying session state
The remediated bridge requires an exact origin and the expected sending window, and still serves the legitimate resize command
The vulnerable preview grants allow-scripts together with allow-same-origin and applies the attribute after the content is assigned
The compensated preview assigns unsanitised markup to a frame whose empty sandbox is set before assignment and before insertion, so the markup cannot execute in the application's origin

calibration.notes: This pack has not completed a reproducible benchmark run and makes no precision or recall claim.

limitations: Browser behaviour varies by engine and version, so a fixture result does not establish behaviour everywhere
Bundlers, server-side rendering, and hydration can change which sink actually executes, so source review alone can mislead
Response headers and framing policies are often set by infrastructure outside the repository and must be observed rather than inferred
A sanitizer's effectiveness depends on its configuration and the context it writes into, neither of which its presence proves
